topics: Conflict and Peace: Pacifism and Just War

data.title: Pacifism and Just War Theory
data.sourcePassage: One of the oldest questions in religious ethics is whether violence is ever morally justified. Two main traditions offer contrasting answers. Pacifism holds that violence is never justified — that the taking of human life is always wrong, and that disputes must be resolved by other means. Religious pacifists draw on powerful teachings: Jesus's command to 'love your enemies' and 'turn the other cheek', the Buddhist first precept of not taking life, and Gandhi's principle of satyagraha — truth-force — which holds that non-violent resistance is more powerful than armed force. Conscientious objectors — people who refused to fight on religious or moral grounds — faced social stigma and sometimes imprisonment in the World Wars. A common misconception is that pacifism is weakness. In reality, non-violent resistance requires enormous courage. Gandhi was assassinated, as was Martin Luther King Jr., who drew on Gandhi's methods in the US civil rights movement. Just War theory takes a different view: that there are circumstances in which the use of force can be morally justified. Developed in Christian thought by Augustine and Aquinas, the theory sets out criteria that must all be met for a war to be considered just. These include: a just cause (defending against attack, not seeking territory or revenge); right intention (restoring peace, not conquest); proper authority (declared by a legitimate government); last resort (all peaceful alternatives exhausted); proportionality (no more force than necessary); protection of civilians; and a reasonable chance of success. If any criterion is not met, the war may not be just. Most wars in history would struggle to meet all these criteria. Just war theory is not a blank cheque for war — it is a demanding standard.

The view that wars should be short and decisive

questions.questionText: What does the 'last resort' criterion in just war theory mean?
options: The war must be the final battle — there can be no further fighting after it
All peaceful alternatives such as diplomacy must have been exhausted before force is used
The last country to be attacked has the right to retaliate
The war must be fought in the country that was attacked, not elsewhere

questions.questionText: Why is pacifism sometimes described as requiring courage rather than being a sign of weakness?
options: Because pacifists often secretly support military action
Because non-violent resistance is physically harder than fighting
Because Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. were assassinated for their non-violent activism
Because conscientious objectors were given dangerous medical duties

questions.questionText: What is proportionality in just war theory?
options: The war must involve equal numbers of soldiers on both sides
No more force than is necessary may be used to achieve the just aim
The suffering caused by war must be proportional to the original crime
The country starting the war must be proportionally larger than its opponent

topics: Conflict and Peace: Religious Teachings on War and Peace

data.title: Religious Teachings on War and Peace
data.sourcePassage: Major world religions offer varied and nuanced teachings on war and peace. Christianity holds a wide range of views. Pacifism has deep roots in Jesus's teaching: 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9); 'Love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44). Quakers and Mennonites maintain absolute pacifism. Mainstream Catholic and Protestant Christianity accepts just war theory — Augustine and Aquinas developed the criteria over centuries. Christianity also emphasises active peace-making: Corrymeela in Northern Ireland worked across Protestant-Catholic divisions; Archbishop Desmond Tutu drew on his Ubuntu theology ('I am because we are') to lead South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission after apartheid. Islam's very name comes from a root related to peace and submission. The greeting 'As-salamu alaykum' (Peace be upon you) is central to Muslim life. Islamic teaching permits defensive war under strict conditions — civilians must not be harmed, trees must not be destroyed, fleeing enemies may not be killed. The overwhelming majority of Muslim scholars condemn terrorism as a distortion of Islamic teaching. The word jihad primarily means inner spiritual struggle; armed defence is the 'lesser jihad' and is subject to the same strict rules as just war theory. Buddhism places ahimsa (non-harm) at the centre of its ethics. The First Precept forbids taking life. Thich Nhat Hanh, a Vietnamese monk, pioneered 'engaged Buddhism' — applying Buddhist compassion to social and political action — during the Vietnam War. Sikhism's concept of Sant Sipahi (saint-soldier) holds that a Sikh should be devout and peaceful but must defend the oppressed if necessary. The kirpan symbolises this duty. Dharam yudh (righteous war) is the Sikh form of just war theory.

Inner spiritual struggle — striving to live according to God's will

topics: Conflict and Peace: Reconciliation and Terrorism

data.title: Reconciliation, Forgiveness, and Terrorism
data.sourcePassage: Reconciliation is the process of restoring a broken relationship after conflict. It is not the same as forgetting what happened, and it is not the same as justice. Reconciliation requires acknowledgement — the harm must be named and owned. It requires accountability — appropriate consequences. And it often involves forgiveness — the victim's release of resentment — which is not the same as condoning the wrong or removing all consequences. Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who chaired South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission after apartheid, argued that forgiveness was essential to peace — not for the sake of the wrongdoer, but for the victim. Hatred and resentment, he argued, destroy the one who holds them. Corrymeela in Northern Ireland has spent decades bringing Protestants and Catholics together, not to ignore what happened during the Troubles, but to build relationships strong enough to survive the truth. Terrorism is the use of violence against civilians to create fear and advance political aims. Students must make critical distinctions here. First, terrorism is condemned by all major world religions — the killing of innocents is explicitly forbidden in Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Buddhism, Hinduism, and Sikhism. When individuals claim religious justification for terrorism, they distort and misuse their tradition. Second, religious motivation is not the same as religious endorsement — a person may claim to act in God's name while doing something their religion forbids. Third, terrorism often arises from complex political, historical, and social grievances; religion may be used as a banner, but is rarely the sole cause. Finally, much terrorism in history has had no religious motivation whatsoever — nationalism, racism, and political ideology have each motivated atrocities. Understanding these distinctions is essential for accurate thinking about conflict and peace.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between forgiveness and justice?
options: Forgiveness removes all consequences; justice means no forgiveness is possible
They are the same thing — you cannot have one without the other
Forgiveness releases personal resentment; justice ensures appropriate consequences — both can coexist
Justice requires punishment; forgiveness requires the wrongdoer to apologise first

questions.questionText: Why did Archbishop Tutu argue that forgiveness was essential to peace in South Africa?
options: Because the law required forgiveness before any prosecution could proceed
Because those who committed apartheid crimes deserved to be freed
Because hatred and resentment destroy the person who holds them — forgiveness frees the victim
Because religious forgiveness is more important than legal accountability

questions.questionText: What does the passage say about terrorism and religion?
options: Some religions permit terrorism in certain circumstances
Terrorism is condemned by all major world religions; those who use religious language to justify it distort their faith
Terrorism is always religiously motivated
Non-religious terrorism does not really exist
Forgetting what happened in order to move forward
Punishing those who caused harm so that justice is done
The process of restoring a broken relationship — requiring acknowledgement, accountability, and often forgiveness
Signing a peace agreement to end armed conflict
